welcome.title: Welcome to AntennaMaster
welcome.body: Plan radio coverage anywhere on Earth. This quick tour shows the essentials — you can leave any time.

simpleMode.title: Simple or Expert
simpleMode.body: New to RF? Start in Simple mode and pick what you want to connect. Switch to Expert for full control.

arrange.title: Make it your own
arrange.body: Click "Arrange panels" to drag the sidebar tools into any order with the ⠿ handle (or the ↑/↓ keys), and hide the ones you never use. Your layout is saved on this device.

place.title: Place your points
place.body: Click the map to drop the transmitter (TX), then the receiver (RX) — or type exact coordinates. The terrain profile appears instantly.

technology.title: Choose a technology
technology.body: Pick a preset — Wi-Fi, 4G/5G, PMR radio, IoT and more. It fills in realistic power, gain and sensitivity for you.

dxf.title: Add local terrain (DXF)
dxf.body: Have a site survey? Upload a DXF to patch high-resolution relief over the global terrain within its footprint.

coverage.title: Run coverage
coverage.body: Simulate a coverage map from the transmitter. Darker blue = stronger signal; transparent = no service.

heatmap.title: Read the heatmap
heatmap.body: Each color band is a signal-margin class. The legend explains them; export the map as PNG, GeoTIFF or KMZ.

glossary.title: Stuck on a term?
glossary.body: Every technical field has an ⓘ icon — hover or tap it for a plain-language explanation, no equations.

glossary.fresnel: Fresnel zone: the rugby-ball-shaped region around the direct ray that carries most of the radio energy. Keep about 60% of the first zone clear of terrain and obstacles, or the link degrades even with line of sight.
glossary.fspl: Free-space path loss: how much a signal weakens just by spreading out in empty space. It grows by 6 dB every time the distance (or frequency) doubles — the baseline every real-world model adds losses on top of.
glossary.kfactor: k-factor: how much the atmosphere bends radio waves. The standard value (4/3) makes the Earth look flatter to radio than to the eye; a low value (worst case) bulges terrain up into the path.
glossary.fade_margin: Fade margin: spare signal (in dB) held back for variability like shadowing and weather. About 5.5 dB gives roughly 90% area reliability, 8 dB about 95%. Zero margin means half of locations will fail.
glossary.sensitivity: Receiver sensitivity: the weakest signal the radio can still decode. It comes from the background noise, the channel width, the receiver's own noise and the quality the signal needs.
glossary.downtilt: Downtilt: aiming the antenna beam slightly below the horizon to focus coverage near the site and reduce interference further away. The main tool for shaping a cell.
glossary.deygout: Diffraction: signal lost when hills or buildings block the direct path. The model finds the strongest obstacles and estimates how much they bend and weaken the signal.
glossary.batch: Batch qualification: check many receiver or subscriber locations against one transmitter at once. Each gets its own terrain profile and a served-or-not verdict, exportable as a spreadsheet.
glossary.clutter: Clutter: extra signal loss from buildings and street furniture that the elevation map cannot see. The percentage is how many locations you want covered — 50% is a typical city, 90% is conservative.
glossary.helmert: Georeferencing fit: how the drawing is aligned to the real world from the reference points you gave. A large error (in meters) usually means a mis-placed point or the wrong units.
glossary.gain: Antenna gain (dBi): how much an antenna concentrates its energy in a direction versus radiating everywhere equally. Higher gain means more reach but a narrower beam.
glossary.txpower: Transmit power (dBm): how much power the radio puts out. More power reaches further, but regulators cap it and it is only one part of the budget.
glossary.itmReliability: ITM answers “the level exceeded at X% of locations and time”, not a bare median. 50% is the median a link budget gives; a coverage commitment is written on 90–95%, which over real terrain roughness costs around 10–15 dB.
glossary.studyRecord: The reference for this exact study: a digest over its complete input set and the build that produced it. It is printed on the exported PDF, and it can be quoted back to retrieve every assumption behind the map — or to re-run the study on its recorded inputs and see whether it still says the same thing.
glossary.p1812Location: ITU-R P.1812 states its answer as “the level not exceeded at X% of locations”, which is the form a coverage obligation is written in. 50% is the median; 95% is the level you can commit to almost everywhere in a pixel, and over real terrain that costs materially more margin.

dxf.uploadHint: Upload a DXF containing relief data (survey points, contour polylines, 3D faces, meshes or spot-height text). It will be fused as a high-resolution patch over the global SRTM base terrain.
dxf.dropBrowse: or click to browse — CRS and units are auto-detected
dxf.autoDetect: Auto-detected: {{mode}} mode, units in {{unit}} — {{reason}}. Adjust below if wrong.
dxf.layersHint: Select the layers that carry terrain elevations. Layers with varying Z values are preselected. {{points}} elevation points selected.
dxf.knownCrsHint: The DXF is drawn in a known projected coordinate system (UTM, Lambert, state plane…). Coordinates are reprojected to WGS84.
dxf.cpHint: Pair 2–3 DXF X/Y locations with their real-world Lat/Lon. A 2D Helmert (similarity) transform is solved by least squares; the residual error in meters is reported after applying.
dxf.originHint: Anchor a known DXF point at a Lat/Lon, give the true bearing of the DXF +Y axis (0° = north-up drawing) and the drawing unit.

indoor.title: Indoor & underground studies
indoor.planIntro: Upload a DXF floor plan, metro station or mine gallery layout. LINE / POLYLINE / ARC entities become walls; assign a material to each layer, click the plan to place the transmitter, then run the multi-wall coverage simulation. No georeferencing needed — everything runs in drawing coordinates.
indoor.floorsTitle: Slabs between TX and the mapped floor — COST-231 penetration (saturates non-linearly)
indoor.floorLossTitle: Per-slab penetration; 18.3 dB = standard concrete slab
indoor.clickToPlace: Click the plan to place TX
indoor.txAt: TX at ({{x}}, {{y}}) drawing units — run the simulation.
indoor.tunnelIntro: Waveguide-regime propagation in a tunnel or mine gallery (Emslie model): free space up to the modal breakpoint, then linear dB/m attenuation. Higher frequencies travel farther — the opposite of open terrain.
indoor.tteIntro: Through-the-earth link (mine paging / cave rescue): a VLF magnetic loop couples through conductive ground. Loss = skin-depth attenuation + near-field (1/r³) spreading — which is why only very low frequencies get through.
indoor.feederIntro: Radiating-cable (leaky feeder) design — pick a catalog cable to autofill real attenuation and coupling specs, then solve amplifier spacing over the run.
indoor.feederConfidence: Planning-level figures for this cable family — confirm the exact SKU's datasheet before design.
indoor.dasIntro: Design a passive DAS over a DXF floor plan: pick the topology (star splitter or corridor cascade of tap couplers), click the plan to place antennas, and the solver computes each antenna's delivered power and EIRP plus the combined heatmap.
indoor.dasClickToPlace: Click the plan to place antennas
indoor.dasPlaceHint: Click the floor plan to add an antenna at that spot (up to 32). Each antenna row sets its gain and the cable feeding it; in cascade mode the tap value is the coupler's tap loss.
indoor.floorsIntro: Stack several storeys of one building: upload a DXF per floor (or duplicate one), place the transmitter on its floor, and every storey gets its own heatmap — its own walls plus the slab loss for the floors crossed.
indoor.floorsTxAt: TX on level {{level}} at ({{x}}, {{y}}) — click another floor's plan to move it

advanced.panelHint: Two-way LMR talk-back, EMF compliance, Longley-Rice (ITM) reliability and the design copilot.
advanced.title: Advanced studies
advanced.needMarkers: Place a TX and an RX marker on the map first.
advanced.twowayHint: Talk-out and talk-in, limited by the weaker direction, with DAQ grading.
advanced.emfHint: ICNIRP / FCC OET-65 exposure exclusion-zone distances — the permitting gate.
advanced.itmHint: Irregular-terrain path loss with a reliability quantile — the statistical model empirical curves lack.
advanced.copilotHint: Runs the profile + height optimizer, then explains the result with quantified fixes.
advanced.p1812Hint: Official ITU-R P.1812 point-to-area path loss (30 MHz – 6 GHz) over the real terrain profile. Enable WorldCover to feed the Recommendation's clutter input from 10 m ESA land cover.
advanced.availHint: Annual availability of a microwave PtP hop (ITU-R P.530 multipath + P.837/P.838 rain), using the hop's real link-budget fade margin over the terrain.
advanced.erlangHint: Erlang trunking dimensioning: blocking (B, calls are lost) or queueing (C, calls wait) probability for N channels, and the channel count a grade of service requires.
advanced.p452Hint: Official ITU-R P.452-18 clear-air interference loss (0.1–50 GHz) between two stations — the coordination number a regulator asks for. Small time percentages capture rare ducting enhancements (the interference worst case). Enable WorldCover to feed the Recommendation's clutter input from real 10 m land cover.
advanced.p2001Hint: Official ITU-R P.2001 wide-range model (30 MHz – 50 GHz, 3 – 1000+ km): one prediction covering the FULL 0–100 % time range — ducting enhancements and deep fades in a single model. This installation reproduces the official ITU validation examples to < 1e-06 dB (see PRECISION_BENCHMARK).
advanced.calibHint: Fit a site correction from real measured RSSI: paste drive/walk-test points below (one per line: lat, lon, RSSI dBm), fit against the prediction from the TX marker, then apply the recommended correction to your coverage studies — predictions become site-tuned.
advanced.needTx: Place the TX marker on the map first.

globe.panelHint: Immersive 3D globe with the Fresnel zone rendered as a glowing tube over real terrain.

lidar.needMarkers: Place TX and RX to run the comparison.

account.title: Account & privacy
account.exportHelp: Everything we hold about your account, as one JSON file: your profile, every saved project with its full study data, and your own activity log. Uploaded drawings and rendered rasters are listed rather than embedded — each stays downloadable from its own page.
account.deleteHelp: Permanently removes your account, your saved projects, your uploaded site drawings and antenna patterns, your rendered coverage results and your logo. Your entries in the organisation's audit log are kept but stop identifying you.
account.deleteConfirmHelp: This cannot be undone. Confirm with your password and type DELETE.
account.erasedDone: Your account and its data have been deleted.

sites.overridesHint: This transmitter runs on its own radio parameters, not the study defaults.
sites.overrideHelp: Per-transmitter radio. Leave a field blank to inherit it from the study, then from the technology preset — that is how one study can hold an 800 MHz macro layer and a 3.5 GHz capacity layer at once.
